reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A group of chronic benign eruptions caused by capillaritis, producing petechiae and golden-brown ('cayenne pepper') pigmentation, most often on the lower legs
Schamberg disease is the commonest variant; other forms include Majocchi (annular telangiectodes), lichen aureus, Gougerot-Blum (lichenoid), and eczematoid-like (Doucas-Kapetanakis) types
Lesions are typically asymptomatic or mildly itchy and are not associated with thrombocytopenia or a coagulation defect
The characteristic colour reflects extravasated red cells and haemosiderin deposition in the dermis
Contributing factors include venous hypertension, gravitational dependency, exercise, and sometimes drugs
Persistent, unusually widespread, or lichenoid variants occasionally overlap with, or should prompt exclusion of, early mycosis fungoides
It is a cosmetic and chronic nuisance rather than a systemic threat, and pigmentation resolves slowly if at all
reference.pathophysiology: Pigmented purpuric dermatoses arise from a lymphocytic capillaritis: inflammation of dermal capillaries increases vascular permeability and fragility, allowing red cells to leak into the papillary dermis. Breakdown of extravasated erythrocytes leaves haemosiderin deposits in dermal macrophages, producing the characteristic golden-brown discolouration overlying fresh pinpoint (cayenne-pepper) petechiae. Platelet counts and coagulation are normal, so the purpura reflects vessel-wall inflammation rather than a bleeding diathesis. Venous hypertension, gravitational stasis, physical activity, and occasionally drug hypersensitivity contribute to the capillary damage.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment with dermoscopy showing coppery-red background and pigment dots
Full blood count and platelet count to exclude thrombocytopenia
Coagulation screen where a bleeding disorder is suspected
Skin biopsy in atypical, persistent, or lichenoid cases to confirm capillaritis and exclude vasculitis or lymphoma
Assessment of venous insufficiency in the lower limbs
Medication review for a possible drug trigger
redFlags: Palpable purpura or systemic symptoms suggesting true vasculitis rather than capillaritis
Thrombocytopenia or abnormal clotting indicating a haematological cause of purpura
Persistent, widespread, or lichenoid patches raising concern for early cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
Progressive change in a long-standing lesion warranting biopsy
reference.prognosis: Pigmented purpuric dermatosis is benign and chronic, often persisting or recurring over months to years; pigmentation fades slowly and treatment is largely cosmetic, but atypical persistent disease occasionally warrants monitoring for mycosis fungoides.
pitfalls: Mistaking benign capillaritis for a bleeding disorder and ordering unnecessary extensive haematological workup, or conversely missing genuine thrombocytopenia
Overlooking an evolving mycosis fungoides in persistent or lichenoid variants
Ignoring contributory venous hypertension and aggravating drugs
